values.value: MCP is the USB-C port for AI
One open protocol, any model, any tool. Here is why the Model Context Protocol is the most important plumbing in AI right now.
Photo by Hal Gatewood on Unsplash

value.markup:
The N×M problem

Before MCP, connecting an AI assistant to something useful — a database, a ticket tracker, a CMS — meant writing a custom integration. Then doing it again for the next assistant. Ten assistants and ten tools meant a hundred brittle adapters, each with its own auth, its own schema, and its own bugs.

The Model Context Protocol collapses that grid. A tool vendor writes one MCP server. An AI host implements one MCP client. Everything that speaks the protocol can talk to everything else. N×M becomes N+M.

values.value: Build the integration once, and every MCP-capable assistant can use it.
The whole point of a standard

value.markup:
Three simple primitives

  • Tools — actions the model can call, described with a JSON schema.
  • Resources — data the host can read into context.
  • Prompts — reusable, parameterised templates a user can pick.

That is genuinely most of it. Small surface area, easy to implement, easy to reason about.

values.value: Many nodes, one shared connection pattern. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash

value.markup:
Why it matters

Because MCP is open and transport-agnostic, it works the same over a local stdio process on your laptop as it does over HTTP in the cloud. Your assistant doesn't care whether it is talking to GitHub, Postgres or Umbraco — it discovers the tools, reads their schemas and gets on with the job.

For vendors, that means one integration reaches every MCP-capable assistant. For developers, it means the assistant you already use can suddenly do real work in the systems you already have. And for everyone, it means less glue code and more time spent on the thing you actually wanted to build.

values.value: Every AI app used to need a bespoke integration for every tool. MCP turns that N×M mess into a single, open plug — and that changes everything about how assistants get work done.

values.value: This blog was built by an AI over MCP
No copy-paste into the backoffice. No custom import script. Just an assistant, a protocol and a CMS that speaks it.
Photo by Edge2Edge Media on Unsplash

value.markup:
From prompt to published

This site started as an empty Umbraco install with a single WWW node. An AI assistant connected to the Umbraco MCP server then:

  1. Created five block element types — Hero, Rich Text, Image, Quote and Blog Post List — and filed them in the Blocks folder.
  2. Configured two Block Grid data types and the Blog Front Page and Blog Post document types.
  3. Imported Unsplash photos into a media folder.
  4. Wrote, structured and published the front page and both posts — block by block.

Every one of those steps is an ordinary management API call, exposed as an MCP tool the assistant can discover and use.

values.value: Structured content, not a wall of HTML. Photo by Chris Ried on Unsplash

value.markup:
Why this is awesome

It respects your model. The assistant isn't pasting HTML into a single text field. It reads the document types, discovers which blocks are allowed where, and writes structured content that editors can keep working with in the backoffice.

It respects your rules. Folders, aliases, media organisation — the same conventions a human developer follows apply to the AI, because it goes through the same API.

It is local and safe. The MCP server runs next to your dev site, talks to it with a scoped API user, and only reads media from folders you explicitly allow.

values.value: The best integration is the one you never had to write.
